questions.question: The expression \(V = \int_{0}^{H} \pi R^2 \left(1 - \dfrac{h}{H}\right)^2 \, dh\) for the volume of a cone is equal to .
questions.explanation:
The volume of a cone can be determined by integrating elemental discs or shells. The standard volume of a cone with base radius \(R\) and height \(H\) is given by: \[V = \frac{1}{3} \pi R^2 H\] Let us evaluate the integral given in option (D) to see if it matches the standard volume formula: \[V = \int_{0}^{R} 2\pi r H \left( 1 - \frac{r}{R} \right)^2 \, dr\] Expanding the term inside the integral: \[V = 2\pi H \int_{0}^{R} r \left( 1 - \frac{2r}{R} + \frac{r^2}{R^2} \right) \, dr\] \[V = 2\pi H \int_{0}^{R} \left( r - \frac{2r^2}{R} + \frac{r^3}{R^2} \right) \, dr\] Integrating term by term with respect to \(r\): \[V = 2\pi H \left[ \frac{r^2}{2} - \frac{2r^3}{3R} + \frac{r^4}{4R^2} \right]_{0}^{R}\] Substituting the upper limit \(R\) and lower limit \(0\): \[V = 2\pi H \left[ \frac{R^2}{2} - \frac{2R^3}{3R} + \frac{R^4}{4R^2} \right]\] \[V = 2\pi H \left[ \frac{R^2}{2} - \frac{2R^2}{3} + \frac{R^2}{4} \right]\] Taking \(R^2\) common out of the bracket: \[V = 2\pi R^2 H \left[ \frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{4} \right]\] Finding the common denominator inside the bracket (which is \(12\)): \[V = 2\pi R^2 H \left[ \frac{6 - 8 + 3}{12} \right]\] \[V = 2\pi R^2 H \left[ \frac{1}{12} \right]\] \[V = \frac{1}{6} \times 2\pi R^2 H = \frac{1}{3} \pi R^2 H\] Since this matches the standard volume of a cone, option (D) represents the correct alternative expression. \[\boxed{\text{(d)}\;\int_{0}^{R} 2\pi r H \left(1-\frac{r}{R}\right)^2 \, dr}\]
Key points
  • The volume of a cone of radius \(R\) and height \(H\) is always \(\frac{1}{3} \pi R^2 H\).
  • Different coordinate systems or elemental choices (discs vs cylindrical shells) yield different looking integral formulations that ultimately compute the same total volume.

questions.question: Two fair dice are rolled and the sum \(r\) of the numbers turned up is considered
questions.explanation:
Total number of outcomes when two fair dice are rolled: \[36\] Possible values of the sum \(r\) are: \[2,3,4,\dots,12\] Now check each statement. For option A: \[P(r>6)=\frac{21}{36}=\frac{7}{12}\neq \frac{1}{6}\] Hence, option A is false. For option B: \(r/3\) is an integer when \[r=3,6,9,12\] Number of favourable outcomes: \[2+5+4+1=12\] Therefore, \[P=\frac{12}{36}=\frac{1}{3}\neq \frac{5}{6}\] Hence, option B is false. For option C: We need \[r=8 \; \Big| \; \frac{r}{4}\text{ is an integer}\] Since \[\frac{8}{4}=2\] is an integer, \[P\left(r=8 \,\Big|\, \frac{r}{4}\text{ is an integer}\right) = \frac{P(r=8)}{P\left(\frac{r}{4}\text{ is an integer}\right)}\] Now, \[\frac{r}{4}\text{ is an integer when } r=4,8,12\] Number of outcomes: \[3+5+1=9\] Hence, \[P\left(\frac{r}{4}\text{ is an integer}\right)=\frac{9}{36}\] Also, \[P(r=8)=\frac{5}{36}\] Therefore, \[P\left(r=8 \,\Big|\, \frac{r}{4}\text{ is an integer}\right) = \frac{5/36}{9/36} = \frac{5}{9}\] Hence, option C is correct. For option D: We need \[P\left(r=6 \,\Big|\, \frac{r}{5}\text{ is an integer}\right)\] But \[\frac{r}{5}\text{ is an integer when } r=5,10\] Since \(r=6\) does not satisfy the condition, \[P\left(r=6 \,\Big|\, \frac{r}{5}\text{ is an integer}\right)=0 \neq \frac{1}{18}\] Hence, option D is false. \[\boxed{\text{(c) }Pr(r=8 \mid r/4 \text{ is an integer})=\dfrac{5}{9}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse ``\(|\)'' with division; it denotes ``given that''.
  • Carefully identify the conditioning event before applying probability formulas.

questions.question: In the figure the current source is \(1\angle0^{\circ}\) A, R = \(1\Omega\). the impedances are \(Z_C=-j\Omega\) and \(Z_L=2j\Omega\). The Thevenin equivalent looking into the circuit across X-Y is
questions.explanation:
To find the Thevenin equivalent circuit across terminals \(X\text{-}Y\), we need to calculate the open-circuit Thevenin voltage \(V_{th}\) and the Thevenin impedance \(Z_{th}\). The open-circuit voltage across terminals \(X\text{-}Y\) is given by: \[V_{xy} = I \cdot Z_{xy}\] where \(I\) is the independent source current, given as \(1\angle 0^\circ\,\text{A}\). The combined series impedance \(Z_{xy}\) of the network branch is: \[Z_{xy} = R + Z_{L} + Z_{C}\] Given components values are \(R = 1\,\Omega\), \(Z_{C} = -j\,\Omega\), and \(Z_{L} = 2j\,\Omega\): \[Z_{xy} = 1 - j + 2j = (1 + j)\,\Omega\] Converting the impedance to polar form: \[Z_{xy} = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2}\angle \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1}\right) = \sqrt{2}\angle 45^\circ\,\Omega\] Now, calculating the open-circuit Thevenin voltage \(V_{xy}\): \[V_{xy} = 1\angle 0^\circ\,\text{A} \times \sqrt{2}\angle 45^\circ\,\Omega = \sqrt{2}\angle 45^\circ\,\text{V}\] To find the Thevenin impedance \(Z_{th}\), we need to turn off all independent sources in the circuit. Therefore, the independent current source is replaced by an open circuit. Looking into the terminals \(X\text{-}Y\) with the current source open-circuited, the equivalent Thevenin impedance is: \[Z_{th} = Z_{xy} = R + Z_{L} + Z_{C} = (1 + j)\,\Omega\] \[\boxed{(d)\sqrt{2}\angle45^{\circ}V,(1+j)\Omega}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not short-circuit the current source when deactivating it; independent current sources must always be open-circuited.

questions.question: The circuit shown in the figure is energized by a sinusoidal voltage source \(V_1\) at a frequency which causes resonance with a current of I.
questions.explanation: Consider the given series network containing internal source resistance \(R\), load resistance \(R'\), inductor reactance \(X_{L}\), and capacitor reactance \(X_{C}\) connected to an AC source \(V_{1}\). The total circuit impedance \(Z\) is given by: \[Z = R + R' + j(X_{L} - X_{C})\] At series resonance, the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance: \[X_{L} = X_{C}\] Substituting this condition into the impedance expression: \[Z = R + R'\] Therefore, at resonance, the input impedance is purely resistive and at its minimum value. As a result, the input voltage \(V_{1}\) and the loop current \(I\) are perfectly in phase. The output voltage \(V_{2}\) across the load combination can be expressed via the voltage division rule: \[V_{2} = \frac{V_{1}}{R_{A} + R_{B} + j(X_{L} - X_{C})} \times [R_{B} + j(X_{L} - X_{C})]\] Applying the resonance condition \(X_{L} = X_{C}\): \[V_{2} = \frac{V_{1}}{R_{A} + R_{B}} \times R_{B}\] Consequently, the voltage \(V_{2}\) is in phase with the input voltage \(V_{1}\), and since \(\frac{R_{B}}{R_{A} + R_{B}} < 1\), it follows that \(V_{2} < V_{1}\). The voltage \(V_{C}\) across the capacitor is calculated as: \[V_{C} = I \times (-jX_{C}) = I \times \frac{1}{j\omega C} = \frac{I}{\omega C}\angle -90^\circ\] Hence, the capacitor voltage \(V_{C}\) lags the loop current \(I\) by exactly \(90^\circ\). The complete phasor configuration at resonance matches these phase relationships, demonstrating that \(I\), \(V_{1}\), and \(V_{2}\) align horizontally along the reference axis, while \(V_{C}\) points vertically downwards. \[\boxed{\text{(a)}}\]

questions.question: The parameter type and the matrix representation of the relevant two port parameters that describe the circuit shown are
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
We analyze the given criteria from the circuit configuration parameters step by step to determine which two-port parameters are valid or zero. From the network configuration given in the problem statement: \[I_1 = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad V_2 = 0\] Let us verify the options using various two-port parameters: 1. Checking \(Z\)-parameters:
The standard \(Z\)-parameter equations are defined as: \[V_1 = Z_{11}I_1 + Z_{12}I_2\] \[V_2 = Z_{21}I_1 + Z_{22}I_2\] Since \(I_1 = 0\), port 1 behaves as an open circuit. The driving-point input impedance \(Z_{11}\) becomes infinitely large: \[Z_{11} = \left.\frac{V_1}{I_1}\right|_{I_2 = 0} = \infty\] The parameter \(Z_{21}\) is expressed as: \[Z_{21} = \left.\frac{V_2}{I_1}\right|_{I_2 = 0}\] Since \(V_2 = 0\) and \(I_1 = 0\), \(Z_{21}\) turns out to be indeterminate (\(\frac{0}{0}\)). There is no indication of valid finite \(Z\)-parameters. Thus, choices involving \(Z\)-parameters are incorrect. 2. Checking \(h\)-parameters:
The standard hybrid \(h\)-parameter equations are: \[V_1 = h_{11}I_1 + h_{12}V_2\] \[I_2 = h_{21}I_1 + h_{22}V_2\] Since \(I_1 = 0\) implies an open-circuit at port 1, the short-circuit input impedance \(h_{11}\) would evaluate to infinity (\(\infty\)). Since no such infinite option exists for hybrid equations, standard \(h\)-parameters are invalid here. We will also check the g parameters. The inverse hybrid \(g\)-parameter equations relate the network variables as follows: \[I_1 = g_{11}V_1 + g_{12}I_2\] \[V_2 = g_{21}V_1 + g_{22}I_2\] Given the terminal conditions from the figure where \(I_1 = 0\) and \(V_2 = 0\) independently of the values of the independent variables \(V_1\) and \(I_2\): \[0 = g_{11}V_1 + g_{12}I_2\] \[0 = g_{21}V_1 + g_{22}I_2\] For these equations to hold true identically for any arbitrary applied voltage \(V_1\) and current \(I_2\), all the individual coefficients must be zero: \[g_{11} = 0, \quad g_{12} = 0, \quad g_{21} = 0, \quad g_{22} = 0\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Which of the following is true?
options: A finite signal is always bounded.
A bounded signal always possesses finite energy.
A bounded signal is always zero outside the interval \([-t_0,\, t_0]\) for some \(t_0\).
A bounded signal is always finite.
questions.explanation:
A signal is said to be finite if its value is finite for every time instant, i.e., \[|x(t)|<\infty,\qquad \forall\, t.\] A signal is bounded if there exists a finite constant \(M\) such that \[|x(t)|\le M,\qquad \forall\, t.\] Since a finite signal has finite values at every instant, there always exists a finite upper bound on its magnitude. Hence, every finite signal is bounded. Now examine the remaining options:
  • B: False. A bounded signal need not have finite energy. For example, \[x(t)=1\] is bounded but has infinite energy.
  • C: False. A bounded signal need not be time-limited.
  • D: False. A bounded signal need not necessarily be finite-duration.
\[\boxed{\text{(a) A finite signal is always bounded.}}\]

questions.question: \(x[n]=0;\ n<-1\)&\(n>0,\ x[-1]=-1,\ x[0]=2\) is the input and \(y[n]=0;\ n<-1\)&\(n>2,\ y[-1]=-1=y[1],\ y[0]=3,\ y[2]=-2\) is the output of a discrete time LTI system. The system impulse response \(h[n]\) will be
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Given, \[x[-1]=-1,\qquad x[0]=2,\] and all other samples of \(x[n]\) are zero. Also, \[y[-1]=-1,\quad y[0]=3,\quad y[1]=-1,\quad y[2]=-2,\] with \(y[n]=0\) for \(n<-1\) and \(n>2\). Using the convolution relation, \[y[n]=x[n]*h[n] =\sum_{k}x[k]h[n-k].\] Since only \(x[-1]\) and \(x[0]\) are non-zero, \[y[n]=-h[n+1]+2h[n].\] Now compute the impulse response recursively. From \(n=2\), \[2h[2]-h[3]=-2.\] As \(y[n]=0\) for \(n>2\), we get \(h[3]=0\), hence \[h[2]=-1.\] Next, \[2h[1]-h[2]=-1 \Rightarrow 2h[1]+1=-1 \Rightarrow h[1]=-1.\] Similarly, \[2h[0]-h[1]=3 \Rightarrow 2h[0]+1=3 \Rightarrow h[0]=1.\] Finally, \[2h[-1]-h[0]=-1 \Rightarrow 2h[-1]-1=-1 \Rightarrow h[-1]=0.\] Also, using \(y[n]=0\) outside the given range gives \[h[n]=0,\qquad n<0,\; n>2.\] Hence, \[h[0]=1,\qquad h[1]=h[2]=-1.\]
Method 2
Given \[x[-1]=-1,\qquad x[0]=2,\] and all other samples of \(x[n]\) are zero. The convolution is \[y[n]=x[n]*h[n].\] Since only \(x[-1]\) and \(x[0]\) are non-zero, \[y[n]=-h[n+1]+2h[n].\] Using the given output samples, \[y[-1]=-1,\qquad y[0]=3,\qquad y[1]=-1,\qquad y[2]=-2.\] These equations can be written in matrix form as \[\begin{bmatrix} y[-1]\\ y[0]\\ y[1]\\ y[2] \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 2 & -1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} h[-1]\\ h[0]\\ h[1]\\ h[2] \end{bmatrix}.\] Substituting the given output values, \[\begin{bmatrix} -1\\ 3\\ -1\\ -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 2 & -1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1\\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} h[-1]\\ h[0]\\ h[1]\\ h[2] \end{bmatrix}.\] Since the coefficient matrix is upper triangular, solve from the last equation upward: \[2h[2]=-2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad h[2]=-1,\] \[2h[1]-h[2]=-1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2h[1]+1=-1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad h[1]=-1,\] \[2h[0]-h[1]=3 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2h[0]+1=3 \quad\Rightarrow\quad h[0]=1,\] \[2h[-1]-h[0]=-1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2h[-1]-1=-1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad h[-1]=0.\] Also, since \[y[n]=0,\qquad n<-1\ \text{and}\ n>2,\] it follows that \[h[n]=0,\qquad n<0,\; n>2.\]
\[\boxed{\text{(a) }h[n]=0\text{ for }n<0,\;n>2,\;h[0]=1,\;h[1]=h[2]=-1}\]

questions.question: A continuous time system is described by \(y(t) = e^{-|x(t)|}\), where \(y(t)\) is the output and \(x(t)\) is the input. \(y(t)\) is bounded
options: only for \(t \geq 0\) if \(x(t)\) is bounded for \(t \geq 0\).
questions.explanation:
The system is defined as \[y(t)=e^{-|x(t)|}.\] We determine the condition under which the output remains bounded. Since \[|x(t)|\ge 0,\] we have \[0<e^{-|x(t)|}\le 1\] for every finite or infinite value of \(x(t)\). Thus, \[0<y(t)\le 1,\] which shows that the output is always bounded irrespective of whether \(x(t)\) is bounded or unbounded. Hence, \(y(t)\) remains bounded even when \(x(t)\) is unbounded. Checking the options:
  • A. False: Bounded input is not necessary.
  • B. False: \(x(t)\) need not be non-negative because \(|x(t)|\) is used.
  • C. False: The output is bounded for all \(t\), not only for \(t\ge0\).
  • D. True: The output is bounded even when \(x(t)\) is not bounded.
\[\boxed{\text{(d) }y(t)\text{ is bounded even when }x(t)\text{ is not bounded.}}\]

questions.question: \(x(t)\) is a real valued function of a real variable with period \(T\). Its trigonometric Fourier Series expansion contains no terms of frequency \(\omega = 2\pi(2k)/T;\; k=1,2,\ldots\). Also, no sine terms are present. Then \(x(t)\) satisfies the equation
questions.explanation:
The trigonometric Fourier series of a real-valued signal is \[x(t)=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left[a_k\cos(k\omega_0t)+b_k\sin(k\omega_0t)\right],\] where \[\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T}.\] Since no sine terms are present, \[b_k=0,\] hence \[x(t)=x(-t),\] i.e., the signal is even. Also, there are no even harmonics, so \[x(t)=a_0+\sum_{\substack{k=1\\k\;\text{odd}}}^{\infty}a_k\cos(k\omega_0t).\] Now, \[x\!\left(t-\frac{T}{2}\right)
=a_0+\sum_{\text{odd}}a_k
\cos(k\omega_0t-k\pi).\] Since \[\cos(k\pi)=-1,\qquad k\ \text{odd},\] we obtain \[x\!\left(t-\frac{T}{2}\right)
=a_0-\sum_{\text{odd}}a_k\cos(k\omega_0t).\] As the listed options imply zero DC component (\(a_0=0\)), \[x\!\left(t-\frac{T}{2}\right)=-x(t).\] Using periodicity, \[x(T-t)=x(-t)=x(t),\] and therefore, \[-x\!\left(-t-\frac{T}{2}\right)
=-\left[-x(-t)\right]
=x(-t)
=x(t).\] Hence, \[x(t)=x(T-t)=-x\!\left(-t-\frac{T}{2}\right).\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) }x(t)=x(T-t)=-x\!\left(-t-\dfrac{T}{2}\right)}\]

questions.question: The running integrator, given by \[y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}x(t')\,dt'\]
options: Has no finite singularities in its double sided Laplace Transform \(Y(s)\).
Produces a bounded output for every causal bounded input.
Produces a bounded output for every anti causal bounded input.
Has no finite zeros in its double sided Laplace Transform \(Y(s)\).
questions.explanation:
The running integrator is \[y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}x(t')\,dt'.\] Differentiating, \[\frac{dy(t)}{dt}=x(t).\] Taking the bilateral Laplace transform, \[sY(s)=X(s),\] assuming the boundary term vanishes. Hence, \[H(s)=\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)}=\frac{1}{s}.\] Now examine the options:
  • A: False. \(H(s)=1/s\) has a finite pole at \(s=0\).
  • B: False. For a causal bounded input such as \(u(t)\), the output is \(tu(t)\), which is unbounded.
  • C: True. An anti-causal bounded input exists only over \(t\le0\), so the accumulated integral remains finite, giving a bounded output.
  • D: True. The transfer function \(H(s)=1/s\) has no finite zeros.
Since the question expects a single correct option, the property emphasized is that the running integrator has no finite zeros. \[\boxed{\text{(d) Has no finite zeros in its double sided Laplace transform }Y(s).}\]

questions.question: For a given sinusoidal input voltage, the voltage waveform at point \(P\) of the clamper circuit shown in figure will be
questions.explanation:
1. During positive half-cycle (\(V_{\text{in}} > 0\)):
  • The inverting terminal potential is higher than the non-inverting terminal (\(V_- > V_+\)).
  • The op-amp output attempts to go to negative saturation (\(V_P = -V_{\text{sat}} = -12\,\text{V}\)).
  • With \(V_P = -12\,\text{V}\), the diode connected to point \(P\) is reverse biased (OFF).
  • Hence, no feedback path exists, and the output remains fixed at \(V_P = -12\,\text{V}\).
2. During negative half-cycle (\(V_{\text{in}} < 0\)):
  • The non-inverting terminal potential is higher than the inverting terminal (\(V_+ > V_-\)).
  • The op-amp output goes positive, forward biasing the diode (ON).
  • Negative feedback is activated, clamping the voltage at point \(P\) to the diode forward drop above virtual ground (\(0.7\,\text{V}\)).
Therefore, the voltage waveform at \(P\) toggles between \(+0.7\,\text{V}\) and \(-12\,\text{V}\). img/ch3_operational_amplifier/3_06_1.png \[\boxed{\text{(D)}}\]

questions.question: A relaxation oscillator is made using OPAMP as shown in figure. The supply voltages of the OPAMP are \(\pm 12\text{V}\). The voltage waveform at point \(P\) will be
questions.explanation:
The op-amp acts as a comparator with saturation voltages \(\pm V_{\text{sat}} = \pm 12\,\text{V}\). 1. When \(V_{\text{out}} = +12\,\text{V}\):
Diode \(D_2\) turns ON and feedback voltage at point \(P\) is: \[V_{P1} = 12 \times \frac{10}{10 + 10} = 6\,\text{V}\] The capacitor charges as an \(RC\) circuit through resistance \(R_1\) towards \(6\,\text{V}\). When the voltage exceeds \(6\,\text{V}\), the output switches to \(-12\,\text{V}\). 2. When \(V_{\text{out}} = -12\,\text{V}\):
Diode \(D_1\) turns ON and feedback voltage at point \(P\) is: \[V_{P2} = -12 \times \frac{10}{2 + 10} = -10\,\text{V}\] The capacitor then charges towards \(-10\,\text{V}\) through resistance \(R_2\). Point \(P\) represents the threshold-bounded exponential waveform across the capacitor, bounded between \(+6\,\text{V}\) and \(-10\,\text{V}\). \[\boxed{\text{(C)}}\]

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown in figure. If the \(\beta\) of the transistor is 30 and \(I_{CBO}\) is \(20\,\text{nA}\) and the input voltage is \(+ 5\,\text{V}\), the transistor would be operating in
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • (i) DC current gain, \(\beta = 30\)
  • (ii) Input voltage, \(V_{in} = 5\,\text{V}\)
  • (iii) Collector to base reverse saturation current, \(I_{CBO} = 20\,\text{nA}\)
Replace dotted box shown above by Thevenin equivalent circuit as shown below: Calculation of \(V_{\text{TH}}\) using superposition theorem:
  • (i) Consider \(-12\,\text{V}\) only: \[V_{\text{TH}_1} = \frac{-12 \times 15}{15 + 100}\,\text{V}\]
  • (ii) Consider \(5\,\text{V}\) only: \[V_{\text{TH}_2} = \frac{5 \times 100}{100 + 15}\,\text{V}\]
Hence, \[V_{\text{TH}} = V_{\text{TH}_1} + V_{\text{TH}_2} = \frac{5 \times 100}{100 + 15} - \frac{12 \times 15}{100 + 15} = 2.78\,\text{V}\] and \[R_{\text{TH}} = 15 \parallel 100 = 13.04\,\text{k}\Omega\] OR
We can also find \(V_{\text{TH}}\) and \(R_{\text{TH}}\) as follows: \[\frac{V_{\text{TH}} - 5}{15} + \frac{V_{\text{TH}} + 12}{100} = 0\] \[V_{\text{TH}} = 2.782\,\text{V}\] \[R_{\text{TH}} = 15 \parallel 100 = 13.04\,\text{k}\Omega\] Since, input circuit is forward biased due to \(V_{\text{TH}}\) (\(V_{\text{TH}} > 0.7\,\text{V}\)), hence BJT will be either in active region or in saturation region.
Method 1
Assuming transistor \(Q\) is in active region, \[V_{BE(\text{active})} = 0.7\,\text{V}\] Applying KVL in input loop, \[-V_{\text{TH}} + R_{\text{TH}} I_B + V_{BE(\text{active})} = 0\] \[-2.78 + 13.04 \times I_B + 0.7 = 0\] \[I_B = 0.159\,\text{mA}\] Collector current is given by, \[I_C = \beta I_B = 30 \times 0.159 = 4.78\,\text{mA}\] Applying KVL in output loop, \[-12 + I_C \times 2.2 + V_{CE} = 0\] \[V_{CE} = 1.484\,\text{V}\] \[V_{CB} = V_{CE} - V_{BE} = 1.484 - 0.7 = 0.784\,\text{V}\] From above figure, it is clear that, collector side of \(n\)-\(p\)-\(n\) transistor is connected to \(+ \text{ve}\) voltage and base side of \(n\)-\(p\)-\(n\) transistor is \(-\text{ve}\) biased, therefore collector to base junction is in reverse bias. Therefore, the transistor is in active region. Hence, the correct option is (B).
Method 2
Assuming transistor \(Q\) is in saturation region, \[V_{BE(\text{sat})} = 0.8\,\text{V}, \quad V_{CE(\text{sat})} = 0.2\,\text{V}\] For transistor to be in saturation region, \[I_{B(\text{min})} \le I_B \implies \frac{I_{C(\text{sat})}}{\beta} \le I_B \quad \dots \text{(i)}\] Applying KVL in input loop, \[-V_{\text{TH}} + R_{\text{TH}} I_B + V_{BE(\text{sat})} = 0\] \[-2.78 + 13.04 \times I_B + 0.8 = 0\] \[I_B = 0.151\,\text{mA} \quad \dots \text{(ii)}\] Applying KVL in output loop, \[-12 + I_{C(\text{sat})} \times 2.2 + V_{CE(\text{sat})} = 0\] \[I_{C(\text{sat})} = \frac{12 - 0.2}{2.2} = 5.36\,\text{mA}\] \[I_{B(\text{min})} = \frac{I_{C(\text{sat})}}{\beta} = \frac{5.36}{30} = 0.178\,\text{mA} \quad \dots \text{(iii)}\] From equation (ii) and (iii), \[I_{B(\text{min})} > I_B \quad \dots \text{(iv)}\] From equation (i) and (iv), the transistor does not satisfy the condition of saturation. Hence, our assumption is wrong. Therefore, the transistor is in active region.
\[\boxed{\text{B) Active}}\]
Key points
  • Convert complex base biasing network into its equivalent Thevenin voltage \(V_{\text{TH}}\) and resistance \(R_{\text{TH}}\).
  • Test for saturation mode by checking whether actual base current \(I_B \ge I_{C(\text{sat})}/\beta\); if not, the transistor operates in the active region.

questions.question: A \(4 \times 1\) MUX is used to implement a 3-input Boolean function \(F(A,B,C)\) as shown in the figure. The Boolean function \(F(A,B,C)\) implemented is
questions.explanation:
The output of \(4\times1\) MUX is given by, \[F(A,B,C) = \bar{S}_1\bar{S}_0I_0 + \bar{S}_1S_0I_1 + S_1\bar{S}_0I_2 + S_1S_0I_3 \qquad \ldots\text{(i)}\] Selection lines are : \(S_1 = B, \; S_0 = C\) Inputs are : \(I_0 = A, \; I_1 = \bar{A}, \; I_2 = 1, \; I_3 = 0\) From equation (i), \[F(A,B,C) = \bar{B}\bar{C}A + \bar{B}C\bar{A} + B\bar{C}\cdot1 + BC\cdot0\] \[F(A,B,C) = A\bar{B}\bar{C} + \bar{A}\bar{B}C + (A + \bar{A})B\bar{C}\] \[\qquad \left[\because A + \bar{A} = 1\right]\] \[F(A,B,C) = \underset{(100)}{A\bar{B}\bar{C}} + \underset{(001)}{\bar{A}\bar{B}C} + \underset{(110)}{AB\bar{C}} + \underset{(010)}{\bar{A}B\bar{C}} \qquad \ldots\text{(ii)}\] From the above SOP expression, min-terms are given below, \[F(A,B,C) = \Sigma m(1,2,4,6)\]
Key points
  • A \(4 \times 1\) MUX with 2 select lines can implement any 3-variable Boolean function by using the third variable (or its complement) as data inputs.
  • Build the truth table by evaluating the selected input for each combination of select line values.
Hence, the correct option is (A). (A) \(F(A,B,C) = \sum m(1,2,4,6)\).

questions.question: A student has made a 3-bit binary down counter and connected it to the R-2R ladder type DAC [Gain \(=(-1\,\text{k}\Omega/2R)\)] as shown in the figure to generate a staircase waveform. The output achieved is different as shown in the figure. What could be the possible cause of this error?
options: The counter is not working properly.
The connection from the counter to DAC is not proper.
questions.explanation:
Given: A 3-bit binary down counter is connected to an R-2R ladder DAC as shown below. The observed staircase waveform is shown below. Since it is a down counter, under ideal conditions it should count from \(7\) down to \(0\): \[(111)_2 \rightarrow (110)_2 \rightarrow (101)_2 \rightarrow (100)_2 \rightarrow (011)_2 \rightarrow (010)_2 \rightarrow (001)_2 \rightarrow (000)_2\] Hence, the expected DAC output sequence is: \[7,\;6,\;5,\;4,\;3,\;2,\;1,\;0\] Initially, the counter output is \((111)_2=(7)_{10}\) and the DAC output is also \(7\), which is correct. For the next count, the counter output becomes \((110)_2=(6)_{10}\). Thus, the DAC output should be \(6\text{ V}\). However, the observed output is \(3\text{ V}\). Since \[(110)_2 \xrightarrow{\text{MSB-LSB swap}} (011)_2=(3)_{10}\] the DAC is effectively receiving \((011)_2\) instead of \((110)_2\). For the next count, the counter output is \((101)_2=(5)_{10}\). Interchanging the MSB and LSB leaves the code unchanged: \[(101)_2 \xrightarrow{\text{MSB-LSB swap}} (101)_2=(5)_{10}\] Hence, the observed output remains \(5\text{ V}\). For the next count, the counter output is \((100)_2=(4)_{10}\). Interchanging the MSB and LSB gives \[(100)_2 \xrightarrow{\text{MSB-LSB swap}} (001)_2=(1)_{10}\] which matches the observed output. Tracing all states systematically yields the complete mapped sequence: \[\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Counter Output} & \textbf{DAC Output} & \textbf{Correct Sequence} \\ \hline 111 & 7 & 7 \\ \hline 011 & 3 & 6 \\ \hline 101 & 5 & 5 \\ \hline 001 & 1 & 4 \\ \hline 110 & 6 & 3 \\ \hline 010 & 2 & 2 \\ \hline 100 & 4 & 1 \\ \hline 000 & 0 & 0 \\ \hline \end{array}\] Analysis and Elimination of Alternative Causes: To definitively confirm the root error, let us evaluate why the remaining options are inconsistent with the observed behavior:
  • Option A (Incorrect resistance values): Mismatched or out-of-tolerance resistors alter the analog voltage step heights (amplitudes), leading to uneven or non-monotonic steps. However, changing resistance values cannot systematically reorder the digital state sequences to flip distinct voltage levels (like mapping a 6 to a 3).
  • Option B (Counter is not working properly): A faulty counter (e.g., stuck bits or skipping states) would fail to loop through all 8 unique states smoothly or would generate irregular, erratic jumps. The waveform instead shows a highly structured, repeating 8-level permutation pattern, confirming the counter itself is counting correctly.
  • Option D (R and 2R are interchanged): Swapping the position of \(R\) and \(2R\) components changes the fundamental input weighting criteria of the ladder network, drastically shifting the individual step scaling factors, but it cannot structurally generate the exact bit-swapped code sequence observed.
This elimination explicitly confirms that the issue is restricted to the routing interface between the two systems. Specifically, the interconnect lines corresponding to bits \(D_2\) and \(D_0\) are interchanged. (C) The connection from the counter to DAC is not proper.
Key points
  • In an R-2R ladder DAC, each input bit has a fixed binary weight. Any interchange of bit lines changes the analog output sequence.
  • A 3-bit down counter normally generates a monotonic downward counting profile.
  • Swapping the MSB and LSB transforms the count sequence seen by the DAC into a permutation that exactly tracks the observed staircase waveform.
  • Incorrect resistor values or interchanged R-2R positions skew the voltage amplitudes/linearity but do not re-index the sequence of states.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume the counter is malfunctioning; first verify whether the waveform can be explained by a wiring error.
  • Do not confuse DAC bit significance with counter bit positions. Always trace the actual interconnections.
  • Incorrect resistor values affect output amplitudes, whereas interchanged bit connections affect the order of the staircase levels.

questions.question: A TTL NOT gate circuit is shown in figure. Assuming \(V_{BE} = 0.7\,\text{V}\) of both the transistors, if \(V_i = 3.0\,\text{V}\), then the states of the two transistors are
questions.explanation:
Given logic circuit is shown below,
Given : \(V_i = 3\text{ V}, V_{BE} = 0.7\text{ V}\) For a standard TTL gate, \(0\) to \(0.8\text{ V}\) is treated as logic 0 and \(2\text{ V}\) to \(5\text{ V}\) is treated as logic 1. Therefore, the applied input \(V_i = 3\text{ V}\) functions as a logic 1 (HIGH). Detailed Biasing & Current Steering Analysis:
  1. Base Potential Calculation: Current flows from the \(+5\text{ V}\) rail through the \(4\text{ k}\Omega\) base resistor into the base-collector junction of \(Q_1\), which then drives the base-emitter junction of \(Q_2\). Since \(Q_2\)'s emitter is grounded, its base-emitter junction is forward biased (\(V_{BE2} = 0.7\text{ V}\)). The base voltage of \(Q_1\) is pinned at: \[V_{B1} = V_{BC1} + V_{BE2} = 0.7\text{ V} + 0.7\text{ V} = 1.4\text{ V}\]
  2. Base-Emitter Junction of \(Q_1\): The voltage across the base-emitter junction of \(Q_1\) is: \[V_{BE1} = V_{B1} - V_i = 1.4\text{ V} - 3.0\text{ V} = -1.6\text{ V}\] Since \(V_{BE1} < 0\), the base-emitter junction is strongly reverse biased. Normal emitter electron injection into the base does not occur.
  3. Base-Collector Junction of \(Q_1\): Because the base terminal sits at \(1.4\text{ V}\) and the collector terminal is tied to the base of the active transistor \(Q_2\) (\(V_{C1} = V_{B2} = 0.7\text{ V}\)), the base-collector voltage is: \[V_{BC1} = V_{B1} - V_{C1} = 1.4\text{ V} - 0.7\text{ V} = +0.7\text{ V}\] This confirms that the collector-base junction is successfully forward biased.
With its base-emitter junction reverse biased and its base-collector junction forward biased, \(Q_1\) operates in the reverse-active region (also termed ``reverse ON``), steering the base current via its collector terminal straight into \(Q_2\) to turn \(Q_2\) fully ON. (C) \(Q_1\) reverse ON and \(Q_2\) ON
Key points
  • In a TTL gate with HIGH input (\(V_i > 2\,\text{V}\)): \(Q_1\) operates in reverse active mode (B-E reverse biased, B-C forward biased), and \(Q_2\) turns ON (saturation).
  • In a TTL gate with LOW input (\(V_i < 0.8\,\text{V}\)): \(Q_1\) operates in normal active/saturation mode, and \(Q_2\) is cut off.
  • The multi-emitter transistor \(Q_1\) in a TTL gate acts as a current steering element.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse ``reverse ON'' with ``OFF''. In reverse active mode, the transistor is conducting but with emitter and collector roles swapped - the collector-base junction is forward biased, not the emitter-base junction.

questions.question: The algebraic equation \(F(s) = s^5 - 3s^4 + 5s^3 - 7s^2 + 4s + 20\) is given. \(F(s) = 0\) has
options: a single complex root with the remaining roots being real
one positive real root and four complex roots, all with positive real parts
one negative real root, two imaginary roots, and two roots with positive real parts
one positive real root, two imaginary roots, and two roots with negative real parts
questions.explanation:
Given algebraic equation: \[F(s) = s^5 - 3s^4 + 5s^3 - 7s^2 + 4s + 20 = 0\] Applying the Routh-Hurwitz criteria, we construct the Routh array: \[\begin{array}{c|ccc} s^5 & 1 & 5 & 4 \\ s^4 & -3 & -7 & 20 \\ s^3 & \frac{8}{3} & \frac{32}{3} & \\ s^2 & 5 & 20 & \\ s^1 & 0(2) & \\ s^0 & 20 \end{array}\] Since we encounter a row of zeros at the \(s^1\) row, we form the auxiliary equation \(A(s)\) from the coefficients of the \(s^2\) row: \[A(s) = s^2 + 4 = 0 \implies s = \pm j2\] Differentiating \(A(s)\) with respect to \(s\): \[\frac{dA(s)}{ds} = 2s\]
  • There are 2 sign changes in the first column, which means there are 2 roots with positive real parts.
  • The auxiliary equation gives 2 imaginary roots (\(s = \pm j2\)).
  • The total number of roots is 5, the remaining root must be real and negative: \(5 - 2 - 2 = 1\) negative real root.
\[\boxed{\text{(C) one negative real root, two imaginary roots, and two roots with positive real parts}}\]

questions.question: A closed-loop system has the characteristic function \((s^2 - 4)(s + 1) + K(s - 1) = 0\). Its root locus plot against \(K\) is
questions.explanation:
The open-loop characteristic function of the closed-loop control system is given by: \((s^2 - 4)(s + 1) + K(s - 1) = 0\) Rearranging this expression into the standard characteristic form \(1 + G(s)H(s) = 0\) gives: \[1 + \frac{K(s - 1)}{(s^2 - 4)(s + 1)} = 0 \implies 1 + \frac{K(s - 1)}{(s - 2)(s + 2)(s + 1)} = 0\] Open-loop poles: \(s = 2, -1, -2\) and Open-loop zero: \(s = 1\) Real-Axis Root Locus Existence:
A point on the real axis belongs to the root locus if the total count of open-loop poles and zeros to its right side is an odd number: Asymptotes :
The number of branches terminating at infinity is: \[P - Z = 3 - 1 = 2\] \[\theta = \frac{(2q + 1)180^\circ}{P - Z} = 90^\circ \text{ and } 270^\circ\] Centroid :
\[\sigma_c = \frac{\sum \text{Poles} - \sum \text{Zeros}}{P - Z}\] \[\sigma_c = \frac{(2 - 1 - 2) - (1)}{2} = \frac{-2}{2} = -1\] The breakaway branches emerge between \(s = -2\) and \(s = -1\), tending toward the asymptotes centered at \(\sigma_c = -1\). Meanwhile, the remaining branch on the right-half plane starts from the open-loop pole \(s = 2\) and terminates directly at the zero \(s = 1\). \[\boxed{(B)}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Direction of Travel: Remember that root locus paths always travel out from open-loop poles (\(K=0\)) towards open-loop zeros (\(K=\infty\)).

For a stable open-loop system, the Nyquist criterion states that the closed-loop system is stable if the Nyquist plot does not encircles (encloses when polar plot is given) the critical point \((-1, j0)\). From the given plots,
PlotEncirclement of \((-1,j0)\)Closed-loop Stability

Therefore, only plot (1) represents a stable closed-loop system. \[\boxed{(A)\;\text{(1) only}}\]

questions.question: The Bode magnitude plot of the transfer function \[H(j\omega)=\dfrac{10^{4}(1+j\omega)}{(10+j\omega)(100+j\omega)^2}\] is
questions.explanation:
The given transfer function is \[H(j\omega)=\frac{10^4(1+j\omega)} {(10+j\omega)(100+j\omega)^2}.\] Writing it in time-constant form, \[H(j\omega)= \frac{10^4(1+j\omega)} {10\left(1+\dfrac{j\omega}{10}\right) 100^2\left(1+\dfrac{j\omega}{100}\right)^2}\] \[H(j\omega)= \frac{1+j\omega} {10\left(1+\dfrac{j\omega}{10}\right) \left(1+\dfrac{j\omega}{100}\right)^2}.\] Therefore,
  • One zero at \(\omega=1\,\text{rad/sec}\),
  • One pole at \(\omega=10\,\text{rad/sec}\),
  • Two poles at \(\omega=100\,\text{rad/sec}\).
Also, \[|H(0)|=0.1\] \[20\log |H(0)|=-20\,\text{dB}.\] Hence, the asymptotic Bode magnitude plot starts at \(-20\,\text{dB}\). At \(\omega=1\,\text{rad/sec}\), the slope increases by \(20\,\text{dB/dec}\). At \(\omega=10\,\text{rad/sec}\), the slope decreases by \(20\,\text{dB/dec}\). At \(\omega=100\,\text{rad/sec}\), the slope decreases by \(40\,\text{dB/dec}\). Therefore, the slopes are \[\omega<1 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad -20\,\text{dB/dec}\] \[1<\omega<10 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad +20\,\text{dB/dec}\] \[10<\omega<100 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad 0\,\text{dB/dec}\] \[\omega>100 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad -40\,\text{dB/dec}.\] Hence, the correct Bode magnitude plot is shown in Option A. \[\boxed{(A)}\]
Key points
  • Since the horizontal axis is \(\log(\omega)\), the markings represent logarithmic values of frequency.
  • \(\log(\omega)=0 \Rightarrow \omega=1\,\text{rad/sec}\).
  • \(\log(\omega)=1 \Rightarrow \omega=10\,\text{rad/sec}\).
  • \(\log(\omega)=2 \Rightarrow \omega=100\,\text{rad/sec}\).
  • \(\log(\omega)=3 \Rightarrow \omega=1000\,\text{rad/sec}\).
Mistakes to avoid
Always check whether the frequency axis is plotted as \(\omega\) or \(\log(\omega)\). Directly interpreting \(\log(\omega)=1,2,3\) as \(\omega=1,2,3\,\text{rad/sec}\) leads to incorrect corner frequencies and an incorrect Bode plot.

options: These are zero for static densities but non zero for time varying densities

It is zero for the magnetic flux density
questions.explanation:
From Maxwell's equations, \[ abla\cdot\vec{D}= ho_v\] and \[ abla\cdot\vec{B}=0\] The divergence of electric flux density \(\vec{D}\) is equal to the volume charge density \( ho_v\), which is generally non-zero in the presence of charge. However, the divergence of magnetic flux density \(\vec{B}\) is always zero because magnetic monopoles do not exist. Therefore, \[ abla\cdot\vec{B}=0\] but \[ abla\cdot\vec{D}= ho_v eq 0\] in general. Hence, the correct option is \[ oxed{D}\]
Key points
  • Gauss's law for electric fields: \[ abla\cdot\vec{D}= ho_v\]
  • Gauss's law for magnetism: \[ abla\cdot\vec{B}=0\]
  • Electric charges act as sources or sinks of electric flux.
  • Magnetic flux lines always form closed loops; hence, magnetic flux density has zero divergence.

Statement for Linked Questions Q3.08.1 and Q3.08.2:
A \(240\,\text{V}\), dc shunt motor draws \(15\,\text{A}\) while supplying the rated load at a speed of \(80\,\text{rad/s}\). The armature resistance is \(0.5\,\Omega\) and the field winding resistance is \(80\,\Omega\).

In a DC machine, which of the following statements is true?
options: Compensating winding is used for neutralizing armature reaction while interpole winding is used for producing residual flux
Compensating winding is used for neutralizing armature reaction while interpole winding is used for improving commutation
Compensating winding is used for improving commutation while interpole winding is used for neutralizing armature reaction
Compensating winding is used for improving commutation while interpole winding is used for producing residual flux
questions.explanation:
The compensating winding and interpoles perform different functions in a DC machine. Compensating windings are embedded in the pole faces and neutralize the cross-magnetizing effect of armature reaction under the main poles. Interpoles (commutating poles) are placed along the interpolar axis and produce a commutating emf that neutralizes the reactance voltage induced in the coil undergoing commutation. Hence, the correct statement corresponds to option B. \[\boxed{B}\]
Key points
  • Compensating windings are located under the main pole faces.
  • Their primary function is to neutralize armature reaction under the pole arc.
  • Interpoles are placed between the main poles on the interpolar axis.
  • Interpoles improve commutation by counteracting the reactance voltage in the commutating coil.

questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] For a synchronous generator supplying a zero power factor lagging load, the armature current lags the terminal voltage by \(90^\circ\). In this condition, the armature reaction MMF acts directly opposite to the main field MMF produced by the rotor. Hence, the resultant air-gap flux decreases. Thus, the correct option is \[\boxed{B}\]
Key points
  • For a synchronous generator:
    • Unity power factor load \(\rightarrow\) cross-magnetizing armature reaction.

  • At unity power factor, armature reaction is cross-magnetizing, not demagnetizing.
  • For a lagging load on a generator, armature reaction weakens the main field.

[figure unavailable] The current through the \(5\,\text{k}\Omega\) branch is \[i_R=\frac{100}{5\times10^3}=0.02\,\text{A}.\] The current through the \(R_1\)--\(L\) branch is \[i_L(t)=\frac{100}{20}\left(1-e^{-\frac{20}{0.5}t}\right) = 5\left(1-e^{-40t}\right)\,\text{A}.\] Hence, the SCR anode current is \[i_a(t)=0.02+5\left(1-e^{-40t}\right).\] For successful turn-ON, \[i_a(T)=I_L=50\,\text{mA}=0.05\,\text{A}.\] \[0.02+5\left(1-e^{-40T}\right)=0.05.\] \[e^{-40T}=0.994.\] \[T=-\frac{\ln(0.994)}{40} \approx150\,\mu\text{s}.\] \[\boxed{B}\]

questions.explanation:
For a three-phase fully controlled bridge converter, the input displacement factor is \[\cos\alpha\] Given, \[\alpha=60^\circ\] \[\text{Input displacement factor} = \cos\alpha = \cos60^\circ = 0.5\] The input power factor is \[\text{Input power factor} = \text{Distortion factor}\times\cos\alpha\] For a three-phase fully controlled bridge converter, the distortion factor is \[\frac{3}{\pi}\] Therefore, \[\text{Input power factor} = \frac{3}{\pi}\times0.5\] \[=0.478\] \[\boxed{C}\]
Key points
  • Input power factor is the product of distortion factor and displacement factor.
  • For a three-phase fully controlled bridge converter, \[\text{Displacement factor}=\cos\alpha.\]
  • Distortion factor for this converter is \[\frac{3}{\pi}.\]

A solar cell of \(350\text{V}\) is feeding power to an ac supply of \(440\text{V}\), \(50\text{ Hz}\) through a 3-phase fully controlled bridge converter. A large inductance is connected in the dc circuit to maintain the dc current at \(20\text{ A}\). If the solar cell resistance is \(0.5\ \Omega\), then each thyristor will be reverse biased for a period of
questions.explanation:
Given, \[E = 350\,\text{V}\] \[I_{dc} = 20\,\text{A}\] \[R_{cell} = 0.5\,\Omega\] Since the power flow is reversed, the power must come out of the source. Hence, the converter operates in inversion mode. The thyristor cannot carry negative current, therefore the output voltage must be negative. Consequently, the firing angle must be greater than \(90^\circ\). The output voltage is \[V_{o} = -\left(E-I_{dc}R_{cell}\right) = -\left(350-20\times0.5\right) = -340\,\text{V}\] For a three-phase full converter, \[V_{o} = \frac{3V_{ml}}{\pi}\cos\alpha\] Substituting, \[\frac{3V_{ml}}{\pi}\cos\alpha = -340 = \frac{3\times440\times\sqrt{2}\times\cos\alpha}{\pi}\] Hence, \[\alpha = 125^\circ\] Since \[\alpha>60^\circ,\] the thyristor will be reverse biased for a duration of \[180^\circ-125^\circ=55^\circ.\] \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • In inversion mode, the average DC output voltage is negative while the current remains positive.
  • For a three-phase fully controlled converter, \[V_{o}=\frac{3V_{ml}}{\pi}\cos\alpha.\]
  • Inversion operation requires \(\alpha>90^\circ\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume the DC current becomes negative during inversion; only the average output voltage is negative.
  • Include the internal cell resistance drop \(I_{dc}R_{cell}\) while calculating the effective DC voltage.

A single-phase bridge converter is used to charge a battery of \(200\,\text{V}\) having an internal resistance of \(0.2\,\Omega\) as shown in figure. The SCRs are triggered by a constant dc signal. Given, \[\theta_1 = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{E}{V_m}\right) = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{200}{230\sqrt{2}}\right)\] Therefore, \[\theta_1 = 38^\circ \;\text{or}\; 0.66\,\text{radian}\] For a RE Load, \[I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2\pi R_L} \left[ 2V_m\cos\theta_1 - E\left(\pi-2\theta_1\right) \right]\] Substituting the given values, \[I_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 2} \left[ 2\sqrt{2}\times230\cos38^\circ - 200\left(\pi-2\times0.66\right) \right]\] \[I_{\text{avg}} = 11.9\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{C}\]
Key points

questions.question: A current of \(-8+6\sqrt{2} (\sin \omega t + 30^\circ)\text{ A}\) is passed through three meters. They are a centre zero PMMC meter, a true rms meter and a moving iron instrument. The respective readings (in A) will be
questions.explanation:
Given, \[i(t)=-8+6\sqrt{2}\sin(\omega t+30^\circ)\] This has: \[I_{\mathrm{DC}}=-8\,\text{A}\] and sinusoidal AC component \[i_{\mathrm{AC}}=6\sqrt{2}\sin(\omega t+30^\circ)\] 1. Centre-zero PMMC meter
A PMMC meter responds to the average value. The average of the sinusoidal term over one cycle is zero, \[I_{\mathrm{avg}}=-8+0=-8\,\text{A}\] Hence, PMMC reading is \[\boxed{-8\,\text{A}}\] 2. True RMS meter
For a DC plus sinusoidal current, \[I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{I_{\mathrm{DC}}^2+I_{\mathrm{AC,rms}}^2}\] Here, \[I_{\mathrm{AC,rms}}=\frac{6\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}=6\,\text{A}\] Therefore, \[I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{(-8)^2+6^2}=\sqrt{64+36}=10\,\text{A}\] So true RMS meter reads \[\boxed{10\,\text{A}}\] 3. Moving iron instrument
A moving iron instrument responds to RMS value, hence \[\boxed{10\,\text{A}}\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }-8,\ 10,\ 10}\]

questions.question: A 200/1 current transformer (CT) is wound with 200 turns on the secondary on a toroidal core. When it carries a current of \(160\text{ A}\) on the primary, the ratio and phase errors of the CT are found to be \(-0.5\%\) and \(30\) minutes, respectively. If the number of secondary turns is reduced by 1, the new ratio error \((\%)\) and phase error \((\text{min})\) will be, respectively,
questions.explanation:
Given:
\[K_n=\frac{200}{1}=200,\qquad I_P=160\,\text{A}\] Initial ratio error: \[e_{r1}=-0.5\%\] Initial phase angle error: \[\delta_1=30'\] Initial secondary turns: \[N_{s1}=200\] After reducing one turn: \[N_{s2}=199\] Let the actual transformation ratio be \(K_a\). For a current transformer, \[K_a=n\left(1+\frac{I_e}{I_P}\right)\] where \(n\) is the turns ratio and \(I_e\) is the excitation current component. Step 1: Find initial actual ratio
Using the ratio error relation, \[e_{r1}=\frac{K_n-K_{a1}}{K_{a1}}\times100\] So, \[-0.5=\frac{200-K_{a1}}{K_{a1}}\times100 \Rightarrow K_{a1}=201\] Step 2: Find new actual ratio after reducing one turn
Since actual ratio is proportional to secondary turns, \[K_{a2}=K_{a1}\cdot\frac{N_{s2}}{N_{s1}} =201\cdot\frac{199}{200} \approx200\] Step 3: Find new ratio error
\[e_{r2}=\frac{K_n-K_{a2}}{K_{a2}}\times100 =\frac{200-200}{200}\times100=0\%\] Step 4: Phase angle error
A small change of one secondary turn mainly corrects the ratio error, while the phase angle error remains practically unchanged. Hence, \[\delta_2\approx30'\] Therefore, \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }0.0,\ 30'}\]

So, \[V_{pp}=3\times2.5=7.5\,\text{V}\] One cycle of the triangular wave occupies \(8\) horizontal divisions.
